name: Penny loafers

card.summary: Laceless leather slip-on shoes with a strap across the vamp, worn to give an outfit a polished, preppy look without the formality of lace-ups.

quick.overview:
Penny loafers are low, moccasin-constructed slip-on shoes with a leather saddle strap across the instep that has a diamond-shaped cutout. They sit between casual and dress footwear, which is why they are used to smarten jeans, chinos or tailoring.

They are a style choice rather than a body modification: the payoff is a neater, more put-together outfit, with colour (brown being more common than black) and material (leather, suede, cordovan) steering how dressy they read.
quick.how: They are worn with or without socks, since socks became optional with loafers from the early 1980s. Brown leather is the usual first pair, and suede and cordovan versions are common alternatives. They are typically paired with chinos, jeans or trousers in casual and business-casual settings.
quick.risks: There are no health risks specific to the style. As with any flat slip-on without laces, fit at the heel and instep matters for comfort and walking; lace-ups remain the norm for the most formal occasions.

lead: Penny loafers are a style of laceless leather slip-on shoe featuring a saddle strap with a cutout across the vamp. Loafers in general have a moccasin-style construction, and the penny version is among the best known.[1]

In menswear they are used to give an outfit a polished but relaxed finish: they are less formal than lace-up Oxfords yet read as more deliberate than sneakers. In the US and Italy loafers are a common casual shoe for both work and leisure.[1]

The first loafers were made in the 1920s in London for King George VI as a casual house shoe, and a Norwegian shoemaker developed the related Aurland shoe from about 1908. In 1934 G.H. Bass of Wilton, Maine began making loafers called Weejuns, a name suggesting Norwegians.[1]

chain: Smarter than sneakers, easier than lace-ups
angle.text: Penny loafers lift casual outfits toward business-casual without laces. Colour and material (brown, black, suede, cordovan) set how dressy the result looks.

paras: Loafers differ by detail. Wildsmith loafers have a serrated seam and reinforced toe box; Aurland shoes have a raised moccasin-like seam; penny loafers add a saddle strap with a cutout; tasseled loafers add tassels on a leather strand; gored dress loafers use elastic side panels and are shaped more like Oxfords.[1]

Wildsmith of London made the first loafer in the 1920s as casual house wear for King George VI, and other London firms sold it as the Harrow.[1] Around 1930 Nils Gregoriusson Tveranger introduced a moccasin-like version of his Norwegian Aurland shoe, which was exported as the Norwegian moccasin and promoted by Esquire.[1] G.H. Bass launched Weejuns in 1934.[1]

The name penny loafer has uncertain origins. A popular account says 1950s prep-school students slid pennies into the strap slot.[1] In 1966 Gucci added a metal horse-bit strap, and the Gucci loafer became a Wall Street staple in the 1970s and 80s.[1]

Brown is more popular than black, and suede and cordovan are common finishes.[1] Socks have been optional since the early 1980s.[1] Although originally men's shoes, penny and tassel loafers are also worn by women.[1] Michael Jackson performed in penny loafers, including many of his dance moves.[1]

timeline.event: Wildsmith makes the first loafer in London.[1]
Tveranger introduces a moccasin-like Aurland shoe in Norway.[1]
Gucci adds a horse-bit strap to its loafer.[1]
